A Self-Defining Operator for Distributed Applications

Shihang Li, Thomas Anderson, Ratul Mahajan, and Simon Peter
University of Washington
© none
Abstract.

To operate distributed applications with high availability, operators must rapidly diagnose and mitigate any incident. LLM-based agents can help, but unlike experienced human operators they do not improve as they handle more incidents. Each investigation starts from scratch, re-deriving likely causes and re-testing hypotheses even when a similar fault was resolved in the past. We present a self-defining operator (SDO) that improves with time by updating its operational behavior and memory. When SDO resolves an incident, it distills that experience into playbooks, which describe reusable diagnostic instructions for future incidents with similar faults, and detectors, scripts that take application telemetry as input and output relevant playbook(s). SDO continuously runs the detectors and invokes LLMs only when one fires, so its token cost scales with incident count rather than with operational time. Across 11 open-source microservice applications, SDO cuts resolution time by 52% on recurring faults while keeping per-incident cost low. SDO is open source at https://github.com/uw-syfi/sdo.

1. Introduction

Distributed applications must remain highly available despite faults in their code, configuration, dependencies, and infrastructure. When a fault degrades an application, operators must restore service quickly; the relevant measure is mean time to resolution (MTTR), the time from incident start until user access to the application is restored (Beyer et al., 2016). Further, because new features are more likely to cause incidents, resolution speed gates the rate at which new features can be deployed while meeting availability goals. Thus, fast resolution of operational incidents becomes a key bottleneck to fully realizing the benefits of higher software development productivity brought about by coding agents.

Today, site reliability engineers (SREs) keep applications healthy (Beyer et al., 2016). What makes an experienced SRE effective is accumulated operational knowledge: how the application is structured, how it has failed before, and what resolved each failure. This knowledge is accumulated in runbooks, standard operating procedures, postmortems, and on-call experience (Beyer et al., 2016). When resolving a new incident, SREs draw heavily on this knowledge base. Production incidents are diverse (Dogga et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2022; Gunawi et al., 2016), but many recur: a root cause, such as a misconfigured resource limit or a broken dependency contract, reappears over time (Zhang et al., 2024), sometimes in new combinations (Dogga et al., 2023; Gunawi et al., 2016). As an SRE operates an application, they learn to recognize these faults and resolve them faster when they recur, driving MTTR down.

AI agents using large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a way to assist SREs. Where earlier automation ran scripts that applied fixes in static scenarios, an agent can handle incidents dynamically by reasoning over ambiguous telemetry, acting on alerts immediately, and using the same logs, metrics, and APIs as human operators. Such agents have begun to appear in research (Chen et al., 2026) and as commercial cloud services (aws, 2025; azu, 2025).

However, unlike experienced SREs, today’s agents do not accumulate operational knowledge. They do not know when the application is degraded as they cannot distinguish good state from bad; human SREs must trigger them manually when incidents occur or set up other triggering infrastructure. And, after they are triggered, they take a long time to resolve incidents as they must reason from scratch, re-examining the application structure, re-deriving likely root causes, and retesting hypotheses even when they have already resolved similar incidents. Consequently, LLM-based agents today are not autonomous, nor do they deliver the MTTR reductions that human SREs achieve from knowledge built up across prior incidents.

We present Self-Defining Operator (SDO), an autonomous and learning operator for distributed applications. It deploys applications from source code and keeps them healthy as incidents occur. SDO does both by building up operational memory, authoring and editing its own application operating procedure as natural-language content and code. As SDO progresses, it increasingly acts using memory rather than reasoning from scratch, resolving recurring faults faster and driving MTTR down as its experience grows. Every piece of learned behavior is human-readable and editable, so human SREs can audit and extend it if needed.

The key challenge in realizing SDO is building reusable memory from past deployments and incidents. To improve over time, SDO must decide what knowledge from each deployment or incident should persist, how to store it in a form it can use later, and when that memory applies in future incidents. This is difficult because the relationship between incidents is not always visible from their surface symptoms: a later incident may affect different resources, combine faults from several prior incidents, or look like an earlier incident at the symptom level despite having a different root cause. At the same time, because SDO runs continuously, it must use resources in a cost-effective way.

To make operational memory reusable, SDO defines two artifacts. A playbook records how to recognize and repair a fault, combining natural-language guidance with scripts for reusable inspection and mitigation steps. Playbooks are parameterized over roles such as the affected service, missing configuration object, or failed dependency, so they apply beyond the specific circumstances of the original incident. Because that parameterization leaves out application-specific context, SDO also maintains an architecture summary: a compact description of the application’s components and dependencies. The summary grounds a playbook’s roles in the current application and is refreshed as the codebase evolves.

To retrieve memory when it is applicable, SDO writes detectors: lightweight non-LLM code that checks over application telemetry. A detector encodes a condition under which one or more playbooks may apply, such as a violated service dependency or missing required configuration. When it fires, the detector returns relevant playbooks and suggests values for playbook parameters, giving SDO a starting point for investigation. Detectors give SDO a cost-effective operating path: steady-state monitoring is code execution, while LLM token cost is paid only for deployment configuration changes and incident work.

SDO applies across the application’s lifecycle. During initial deployment, SDO authors the deployment artifacts that bring the application up and defines generic detectors that monitor error rates for end-user functionality. Once the application is live, SDO runs a Kubernetes controller for ongoing monitoring and incident response: a monitor evaluates the initial detectors and invokes the LLM when they report degradation. Thus, before SDO has learned any fault-specific repair, an incident can still trigger open-ended investigation. As incidents are resolved, SDO adds fault-specific detectors that surface matching playbooks. SDO writes detectors as code against a fixed detector API it cannot modify, and writes playbooks and the architecture summary as version-controlled files in the application repository.

This paper makes three contributions:

  • We design SDO, an autonomous operator that brings a Kubernetes application from source to production and keeps it healthy by authoring its own operating procedure as executable, versioned operational memory: playbooks that capture reusable repairs, detectors over live cluster state that surface the playbooks that apply, and an architecture summary that models the application.

  • We implement SDO as a Kubernetes controller centered on a monitor that runs agent-authored detectors over live cluster state with no LLM on the steady-state path, and a write path that commits all memory to the application repository as auditable source.

  • We evaluate SDO on SREGym (Clark et al., 2026), a benchmark for agents that diagnose and repair faults in Kubernetes applications. We extend it to support deploying applications from source and to generate new incident variants from its original faults. Across 11 open-source applications, accumulated memory in SDO cuts MTTR by 52% on recurring faults, including ones that resurface with different symptoms, while detector-based retrieval stays accurate and cheap as memory grows, keeping operating costs low.

2. Requirements for Autonomous Operators

Operating a production application is continuous work that spans its life: deploying it, keeping it healthy as faults arise, and scaling and evolving it as the code or workload changes. When an incident occurs, operators work through a well-established sequence (Beyer et al., 2016). They detect the anomaly through alerts, dashboards, or user reports; localize the affected component by narrowing from the whole system to a service, pod, or configuration file; perform root-cause analysis to determine the underlying cause; and mitigate by applying a fix, such as updating a manifest, restarting a service, or rolling back a recent change, then verify that the system returns to health. This happens under time pressure. Every minute of an outage interrupts users and erodes trust, and outages remain common and costly across the industry (Uptime Institute, 2024; Dogga et al., 2023).

An autonomous operator must work across this full operational lifecycle. To do so efficiently, it must meet three requirements. (1) It must own detection rather than wait for an external alerting stack or a human to flag the problem. Waiting introduces latency and a dependence on external systems. (2) It must accumulate knowledge across incidents. Fault classes recur, and linking a new incident to a related past one measurably reduces the effort to resolve it; gaps in this knowledge are a leading cause of delayed mitigation. (3) It needs to operationalize memory to make it efficient to retrieve when needed. Simply using an LLM to continuously reason about system state is prohibitively expensive given how rarely faults occur relative to uptime. Together, these requirements define the gap between an agent that merely responds to incidents and one that operates an application continuously across its life. We elaborate on these insights in the rest of this section.

Production incidents are diverse but patterned.

Operating an application is challenging, as production faults are diverse. Large-scale studies of cloud incidents converge on a broad taxonomy of root causes: code defects, configuration errors, failed or partial upgrades, broken dependencies between services, resource exhaustion, and infrastructure faults (Gunawi et al., 2016; Gunawi et al., 2014; Dogga et al., 2023). The distribution is dominated by causes outside application code: in one study of high-severity incidents, roughly 60% were root-caused to non-code issues such as service dependencies, infrastructure, deployment, and configuration (Ghosh et al., 2022). Configuration in particular is a persistent source of failure, where a single mis-set or missing field can take down a dependent service (Yin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2021).

Failures are also frequently not fail-stop, so a fault can degrade behavior while the system keeps running and the symptom may be noticed late (Cotroneo et al., 2019). Effects propagate across service boundaries, so the component where a problem surfaces is often not the one at fault (Cotroneo et al., 2019; Maurer, 2015). Symptoms are often noticed via partial, noisy signals, and the space of plausible causes is large. Without prior knowledge of the specific application, an investigator cannot tell which to pursue first (Zhou et al., 2021).

Incidents are also not independent draws. The same root-cause classes reappear throughout multi-year studies of production outages (Gunawi et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2020). But the relationship between a past incident and a present one is rarely a surface match: the same root cause can present through different symptoms, a single incident can combine several causes, and superficially similar incidents can have unrelated causes (Dogga et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2020). Genuinely novel faults also occur. Hence, prior knowledge works only when it applies without replacing investigation.

Human operators get more effective with experience.

Operators have developed practices to cope with these conditions, and they center on reusing knowledge from past incidents (Beyer et al., 2016; Beyer et al., 2018). The most direct expression is recognition: an engineer who has seen a fault class before identifies it from its symptoms and checks the likely cause directly, skipping the "first principles" investigation a newcomer would perform (Beyer et al., 2016). Underlying this is a mental model of the application, including service dependencies, configurations, and past failures.

Other tools and practices come into play as well. Runbooks codify the mapping from known symptoms to diagnostic steps and proven fixes. Postmortems convert each incident into a durable record of what failed and how it was resolved (Beyer et al., 2016; Beyer et al., 2018; Maurer, 2015). On-call rotations then spread this context across a team (Beyer et al., 2018). The value is measurable: linking a new incident to related past ones reduces the effort to mitigate it (Chen et al., 2020; Saha and Hoi, 2022), while gaps in this operational knowledge are a leading cause of delayed mitigation (Ghosh et al., 2022). For example, Google reports that a good playbook lowers mean time to repair by roughly 3×\times (Beyer et al., 2016).

Current SRE agents start incidents cold.

LLM-based agents are a natural fit for this work. Where earlier automation ran fixed scripts and controllers that handle only the conditions their authors anticipated, an agent reasons over ambiguous cluster state and traverses the same diagnostic loop a human would over the same logs, metrics, and APIs. Such agents have begun to appear, as research root-cause analysis assistants (Chen et al., 2024; Roy et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), multi-agent diagnosis systems (Chen et al., 2026), and commercial cloud services (aws, 2025; azu, 2025). These systems share a per-incident interaction model: an incident is surfaced, usually by the existing alerting stack (OpenTelemetry Authors, 2025; Prometheus Authors, 2025; PagerDuty, 2025; Grafana Labs, 2025; Jaeger Authors, 2025; Datadog, 2025; Dynatrace, 2025; New Relic, 2025; Splunk, 2025; Honeycomb, 2025; incident.io, 2025; Zenduty, 2025; FireHydrant, 2025; Amazon Web Services, 2025; Google Cloud, 2025; Microsoft, 2025), and an agent is dispatched to diagnose and repair the incident. Working context is discarded afterwards. Each is, in effect, a freshly hired on-call engineer for a single incident.

3. SDO Design

SDO is an autonomous operator for distributed applications run via Kubernetes. It learns from the incidents it resolves, and each resolution updates operational memory, making the next related incident faster to handle. §2 places three requirements on SDO’s design. First, SDO must autonomously operate an application, from deploying it from source to operating it continuously. Second, it must distill reusable lessons from each incident, and it must retrieve and apply that lesson when a related fault recurs. Third, it must do both at low cost.

SDO meets these requirements as a long-running agent that defines itself. It authors code and instructions that determine its runtime behavior. In steady state, SDO runs self-authored code that decides when to dispatch subagents. A dispatched subagent uses an LLM to take actions, guided by instructions authored by earlier invocations, and in turn revises both the instructions and the dispatching code.

One principle runs through the design: SDO prescribes the interface for learning, while subagents do the learning. SDO fixes the form operational memory can take, the interfaces subagents write against, and what a memory artifact must satisfy before it is committed.

Overview.

Figure 1 shows an overview of SDO. When the application is not yet running, a human-provided deployment objective brings it from source to a healthy deployment (§3.1). Once it is live, a monitor watches application health and dispatches a responder subagent as incidents arise (§3.2). After resolving an incident, the responder reflects, by distilling what the session learned into operational memory. A code commit deploys the resolution, while refreshing memory so it stays aligned with the application (§3.4).

SDO’s operational memory, the knowledge it accumulates, has five kinds of artifacts: playbooks, detectors, an outcome log, an architecture summary, and a health objective. The architecture summary captures the application’s logical structure, such as its services and the dependencies between them, while the health objective captures human-provided input defining healthy operations for the application (§3.1). A playbook contains reusable repair instructions generalized from a resolved incident (§3.2). A detector is non-LLM, runnable code over cluster state that quickly detects a fault and surfaces the playbooks relevant to addressing it (§3.3). For example, a detector might flag any deployment that references a missing Kubernetes ConfigMap. Finally, the outcome log marks each incident response as a success, a false positive (FP), or a false negative (FN), used by SDO to refine its detectors (§3.4). Memory artifacts are maintained as durable text files, enabling human operators to read, edit, or seed any artifact.

3.1. Application Deployment

Initial deployment is where SDO first populates operational memory. The human operator gives SDO a natural-language health objective: a definition of what it means for the application to be healthy, the public-facing endpoints it must expose, and any other requirements (e.g., which services to co-locate). From this objective, SDO brings the application from source to a running state that satisfies it. It does this with two subagents: a deployer produces the artifacts needed to run the application together with an architecture summary that models it, and a health judge checks whether the application is healthy. The two subagents iterate: the deployer brings the application up, the judge decides whether it is healthy, and the deployer revises until it is. Bringing an application up takes many iterations, enough that the detail accumulated across them would overrun a single context window; SDO therefore starts each role with a fresh context on every handoff and carries continuity only through the architecture summary and objectives.

The deployer.

The deployer produces the architecture summary, capturing the application’s main components, their relationships and dependencies, their configuration, and the build graph. The summary is small by construction and orients the deployer toward a working deployment without re-reading the source across attempts. The deployer commits each attempt, so a later subagent session, started fresh, recovers from the summary and its own committed history. From this understanding, it authors the deployment artifacts such as Kubernetes manifests and brings the application up.

The health judge.

The health judge uses the human operator’s definition of what it means for the application to be healthy to author programs that decide whether the application has reached a healthy state: programmatic checks over cluster and application-level state. The judge then identifies failure patterns the checks would miss and revises them to handle those patterns, iterating until the checks are robust. These checks are SDO’s first detectors: they measure application health rather than look for any specific fault. During deployment they are the success signal. The application is up when they all report healthy, and the deployer and judge iterate until they do. Once the application is live, they become a safety net. Any fault that manifests in observable state, whether as degraded user-facing behavior or as divergence from the application’s desired state, trips one of them and dispatches a responder. Because they are anchored in the human operator’s objectives and authored by a role separate from the responder that repairs incidents, they remain an independent measure of health that the responder cannot redefine to declare premature victory.

3.2. Response to New Incidents

Once the application is live in production, incidents may arise. The monitor dispatches a responder when a detector fires (§3.3 describes how SDO detects incidents and dispatches responders). The generic health detectors authored during deployment (§3.1) are always present, so any fault that degrades application health dispatches a responder even before a fault-specific detector exists. The human operator can also dispatch a responder directly for a fault the health detectors miss; SDO logs the miss as a false negative and authors a detector for it (§3.4). The responder’s measure of success is every detector returning to a healthy report; the responder works until no detector fires.

Quick playbook check.

The responder browses the playbook library first. Browsing is tiered so it stays cheap as memory grows. SDO keeps an index that names each playbook with a one-line description of the fault it repairs. The responder reads this index first, opening a playbook’s guidance only when its index entry looks relevant and descending into its scripts only when that guidance fits the current cluster. The responder thus scans the whole library without reading every playbook in full.

Hypothesis-driven investigation.

If no playbook is found (the default upon first deployment), the responder investigates from live cluster state with an iterative hypothesis-revision loop. Each round forms a candidate cause from the current symptoms and the architecture summary, then tests it: if this cause were the fault, the cluster would exhibit some observable consequence, which the responder checks for, confirming the cause or eliminating it and forming a revised hypothesis. Once a cause is confirmed, the responder mitigates it. Because a complex incident can stem from several contributing causes, the responder keeps forming, testing, and mitigating until every detector reports healthy. The architecture summary seeded at deployment (§3.1) bounds the candidate causes to those consistent with the application’s structure. The responder can spawn subagents to pursue competing hypotheses concurrently, each returning only its conclusion so the parent’s context stays focused.

When the responder needs to check a property of the cluster, it authors a parameterized script, runs it, and keeps the script if it proves useful. This is similar to how SREs accumulate shell scripts across incidents. Suspecting a configuration problem, for instance, the responder could write a script to enumerate a service’s ConfigMap references and report missing targets, run it against the crash-looping service, and confirm the missing reference. When it later reflects, the responder keeps successful scripts as part of the playbook.

Post-fix reflection.

A successful session ends with a reflect step. Because the responder that just handled the incident does the reflection, its decisions are still in context, and it abstracts the resolution directly. As it reflects, the responder distills the resolution into a playbook and authors a detector that can flag this fault going forward. The responder commits the new playbook and detector to the repository, and a redeploy registers the detector with the monitor. SDO only commits valid detectors: a detector must compile against the SDO-prescribed interface, and each playbook it names must exist. From this point the fault is covered: a recurrence trips the detector rather than requiring another open-ended investigation, the monitor surfaces the relevant playbooks, and the responder decides whether each one applies to the current incident.

3.3. Fast Response to Known Incidents

Detectors flag incidents, surface playbooks.

Given a known incident, a corresponding detector surfaces relevant playbooks. To do so, a detector declares two things: the cluster state it reads, which tells the monitor when to re-run the detector, and the playbooks it may surface. Its logic decides, from the state it reads, whether its condition holds and which of its playbooks to surface. To help the responder, a detector may also localize the condition by naming the offending object and any related objects. In other words, detectors are pure functions over cluster state, using accessors to the application’s services, pods, deployments, ConfigMaps, endpoints, and events (see Listing 1 for an example). A detector reads cluster state by default. For a signal that is not in cluster state, such as an application-level latency metric, a reflecting responder may author a telemetry, integrated with standard observability tooling (Prometheus Authors, 2025; OpenTelemetry Authors, 2025), that feeds the signal into the queryable view, so the detector surface grows with the application.

Detectors are cheap and robust.

Because a detector is deterministic code over structured state, the monitor evaluates it on its own schedule without any LLM call, making it cheap. Steady-state cost is therefore detector evaluation alone. LLM token cost scales with the number of incidents rather than with operating time.

Only a detector that fires persistently across evaluations dispatches a responder, with the recent evaluation history and the conditions it flagged provided as initial context. A transient failure that clears on the next evaluation is treated as a fluke. Detector evaluation is deterministic: the same cluster state always yields the same result. In our example (Listing 1), when the fault recurs on a different deployment, the detector names the deployment and the absent ConfigMap, and the responder binds the playbook’s parameters to them, mapping each parameter to the resource the detector flagged.

Playbooks guide from root cause to resolution.

The responder confirms the surfaced playbooks against current state. Once they are confirmed, it runs the relevant playbooks to yield a resolution. Playbooks have two components. The first is a pair of natural-language instructions: how to decide whether the current cluster has the root cause this playbook describes, and, if it does, how to repair it. The second is a set of shell scripts the responder can run to inspect the live cluster to help it determine the root cause. Both the instructions and scripts use placeholder names rather than literal resource names, so a playbook applies to any later incident with the same root cause regardless of which specific services or configuration objects are involved. Reflection chooses what to parameterize.

Fixes are double-checked.

The session ends when detectors report the application healthy again. In this case, the responder commits the repair as a source change and redeploys. Confirmation guards the repair: the responder re-checks the condition the playbook assumes, here that the named ConfigMap is indeed absent, before acting, and if the condition does not hold, the session falls back to the open-ended investigation of §3.2. When several faults coincide, say a missing ConfigMap on one service and a port misconfiguration on another, several detectors fire at once, and the monitor batches them into one session in which the responder applies each surfaced repair, bound to its own resources.

3.4. Refining Memory Over Time

Applications change over time. Hence, SDO evolves its memory to keep it aligned with the live application. To do so, it refines detectors based on incident outcomes and it revises the architecture summary with new repository commits.

Refining from outcomes.

A detector can map to its playbooks too broadly or too narrowly, and SDO has a signal for each. A detector is too broad when it fires but the responder, on inspection, finds its condition absent and applies no playbook. For example, the missing-ConfigMap detector might flag a reference marked optional, which is not a fault. It is too narrow when the responder resolves a fault with a playbook that the detector failed to surface, reaching it only by open-ended investigation.

SDO records both signals: for each session, SDO logs which detectors fired and which playbooks the responder applied, and commits this append-only outcome log to operational memory. The responder reads this log when it reflects and may adjust the mapping, tightening or splitting a detector that fired too broadly and widening one that fired too narrowly. Over successive incidents this sharpens the detector-to-playbook mapping. The same log grounds structural edits: detectors that fire together across sessions suggest one root cause to merge, and a detector that leads to divergent repairs suggests two to split.

Keeping memory aligned.

Each architecture summary is tagged with the Git commit at which it was generated. On a later commit, SDO passes the diff against that commit to the responder at its next reflection, which classifies whether the change is topology-relevant (services added or removed, dependency edges changed, configuration keys renamed) and regenerates the affected portion of the summary if so. Playbooks and detectors whose referenced entities the diff removed or renamed are marked for review, which the agent revisits at its next reflection.

SDO does not retire memory by disuse. Operational knowledge has a long-tail value distribution: a playbook that applies once a year is precisely the entry a responder could not reason about from first principles, yet usage-based pruning (LRU, frequency thresholds) would retire exactly these rarely-used entries. SDO refines an entry that proves wrong, through the false-positive and false-negative signals above, and retains an entry that stays quiet. Memory changes only through edits the agent makes during reflection.

4. Implementation

SDO is split into an agent runtime and a controller. The agent runtime is approximately 6,000 lines of Python; the monitor and detector runtime is a Kubernetes controller written in approximately 3,000 lines of Go. The agent runtime exposes a generic interface that decouples SDO from any single agent implementation. We provide two backends: our own harness built on the Pydantic AI agent framework (pyd, 2025), and a portable adapter that drives off-the-shelf coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode. The agent has standard coding-agent tools, a shell and file read/write primitives, and it may spawn nested agents within a session. No agent carries state between sessions.

Standardized agent interactions.

SDO standardizes the interactions it requires of an agent through Model Context Protocol (MCP) (Anthropic, 2025) servers, so any backend behind the agent interface participates identically. The agent reports the structured outcomes SDO depends on through these servers, for instance recording that it has reached a diagnosis. SDO also exposes CLI tools the agent may run while editing memory, such as checking that a detector compiles and that it only references previously saved playbooks. The agent invokes these checks itself, and SDO guards the commit path to reject any change that fails them, so a session cannot persist memory that breaks these validity checks.

Monitor and detectors.

The monitor runs in the controller and reads cluster state through the Kubernetes API. Each detector is compiled into the controller and loaded from the repository, and it declares the resource kinds it reads and the interval at which it runs (§3.3). The monitor evaluates each detector on its interval, snapshotting a read-only, typed view of the cluster state and passing it to the detector (the Cluster value in Listing 1).

Externalizing memory.

SDO stores its memory in the application’s Git repository: the architecture summary and playbooks as Markdown (with each playbook referencing its scripts by path), the scripts as their own files, and detectors as Go source. The agent reads and writes this tree with file primitives and commits changes with git; a redeploy compiles and registers any new or changed detectors with the monitor. We chose a plain file tree over an embedding store: the rapid adoption of agent skills (age, 2025), which organize domain knowledge as file-tree hierarchies, shows that such layouts are effective for LLM retrieval while remaining human-readable and version-controllable. Keeping memory in the repository also makes every change to the operator’s behavior an auditable commit.

5. Evaluation

We evaluate SDO to answer four questions:

  1. 1.

    Do the speed and effectiveness of end-to-end incident response improve as SDO accumulates memory? (§5.1)

  2. 2.

    Can SDO deploy applications reliably and efficiently? (§5.2)

  3. 3.

    Does learned operational memory improve resolution of unseen recurrences without degrading performance on novel faults? (§5.3)

  4. 4.

    Do detectors retrieve relevant operational memory accurately and cheaply? (§5.4)

Benchmark.

We evaluate incident resolution on a variant of SREGym (Clark et al., 2026), a benchmark of 90 fault-injection problems spanning distinct root causes across multiple microservice applications deployed on Kubernetes. Each scenario introduces a fault, such as a misconfiguration, resource constraint, or dependency failure, into one or multiple running applications. It measures whether an agent can diagnose the root cause and mitigate it by resolving the fault. By design, SREGym starts each incident scenario from scratch, by redeploying the involved applications. However, SDO may retain operational memory across scenarios.

Across the evaluation, we use 11 open-source microservice applications (Table 1). The incident-resolution experiments apply fault scenarios derived from SREGym’s problem suite to four of these applications (marked in Table 1); the deployment experiment uses all 11 applications to stress deployment from source.

We extend SREGym in two ways to create more diverse fault scenarios. First, we analyze the 90 faults in SREGym and use them to create fault templates, which permute an original SREGym problem along a common set of axes: the application and service(s) that are impacted by the fault, and one or more fault-specific parameters (e.g., port numbers, environment variable names and values). Using these fault templates, we generate different variants of the same fault, where each fault impacts the deployed application in a different way, depending on the fault parameters that are used. Second, we compose multiple faults into a single incident. We create an incident stream generator that creates new incidents by composing one or more faults generated from the above templates. The incident stream is computed deterministically given the same seed.

Agent harness.

Across all experiments, every agent is instantiated with Claude Code using Claude Sonnet 4.6. Baselines differ only in the memory available to the agent and in the mechanism used to retrieve that memory; unless stated otherwise, they use the same model, tools, Kubernetes access, and benchmark interface.

5.1. Incident Resolution Effectiveness

We first investigate whether SDO improves end-to-end incident response as it accumulates fault-specific operational memory. To do so, we evaluate the aggregate learning curve over a deterministic stream of 200 incidents, where each incident may involve one or multiple of the four fault-target applications (Table 1). Each incident deploys its target applications, injects its composed faults, and tears the applications down after resolution. We replay the identical stream for every configuration. SDO builds operational memory per application in each application repository. Each agent is given repositories of the applications involved in the incident.

Metrics.

We measure incident resolution effectiveness via the following metrics. Time to resolution (TTR) is the end-to-end time from incident start to resolution, where the incident starts when SREGym injects the faults into the application, and is marked resolved when the agent submits a benchmark-specific tool call indicating resolution. Solve rates report diagnosis success, mitigation success, and end-to-end success. Diagnosis success tests whether the agent identified the correct root causes for the faults; mitigation success tests whether the agent remediated the faults; end-to-end success requires both. Token usage is the total number of LLM tokens consumed while resolving each incident.

Baselines and configurations.

We compare four configurations. Memoryless is Claude Code with no persistent incident memory, matching the best-performing SREGym baseline (Clark et al., 2026). History-Embed and History-LLM are baseline memory systems that store prior incident histories. Each incident is stored in two layers: the full trajectory of the agent’s incident response and a short summary generated by the agent. History-Embed retrieves histories by a popular embedding and vector retrieval configuration: we use BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5 (Xiao et al., 2023) to compute each incident summary’s embedding and Qdrant (Qdrant, 2025) for document indexing and retrieval, returning the top five histories by similarity. History-LLM mimics an emerging pattern of retrieving knowledge in agent context (e.g., agent skills (age, 2025)): the agent directly reads the summaries and chooses histories that are relevant to the current incident. In both variants, the agent can grep over retrieved trajectories.

Results.

All systems see substantial per-incident variance because the incident generator composes different numbers and kinds of faults into each problem. We compare configurations on the same incident sequence and focus on trends and distributions rather than individual incidents. Figures 2 and 3 report rolling-average timelines (window of 30 incidents) and distributions of TTRs and token usage, and Table 2 reports solve rates for the entire incident stream. We find that SDO resolves incidents faster and cheaper as it accumulates memory. Early in the stream, SDO behaves like the baselines because it has little fault-specific memory. As detectors and playbooks accumulate, the rolling TTR drops below all baselines, and token usage falls with it.

The improvement comes from two coupled mechanisms: detectors reduce search, and playbooks reduce resolution work. First, detectors retrieve the relevant memory cheaply and localize it to the resources implicated by current cluster state. Second, the playbook turns prior work into reusable procedure. The agent still reasons over the live cluster and can reject a misleading playbook when evidence contradicts it, but a correct playbook shifts much of the work from generating new shell commands and hypotheses to invoking agent-authored scripts with the right parameters.

The right panel of Figure 2 shows how SDO’s memory grows over the stream. Early incidents add playbooks and detectors rapidly: with little memory to draw on, SDO investigates from scratch and distills each resolution into new memory, sometimes adding several playbooks and detectors at once when an incident exposes independent faults. Detectors stay fewer than playbooks because they key on symptoms while playbooks key on root causes, and distinct root causes can manifest the same symptoms. Over incidents, SDO keeps improving the entries it already has, refining playbooks and merging redundant ones. Inspection of the repository git history shows this consolidation: agents repeatedly refactored command sequences they had run as sequential shell calls into reusable playbook scripts, which grew into broader utility tools with subcommands and flags for common diagnostic and mitigation tasks. Agents revised the playbook text to call these tools directly; a later entry, for example, runs one subcommand to test connectivity and another to enumerate affected containers on a dependency failure. In effect, SDO builds a small suite of operational CLI tools that speed its interaction with the cluster.

Memoryless shows the cost of having no accumulated operational state. Memoryless has high variance from problem difficulty, but its rolling TTR and token usage are flat. It carries no state between incidents, so it repeatedly pays the same orientation and investigation cost.

History-Embed shows that cheap retrieval is not enough when memory is stored as raw incident history. History-Embed has TTR and token profiles similar to Memoryless, but a lower solve rate. Its retrieval operates over raw incident histories, so symptom-similar incidents can outrank incidents with the same root cause, and many near-duplicate past incidents reduce retrieval diversity as memory grows. When the retrieved summary does not match current cluster state, the agent often ignores it and falls back to scratch investigation. Its solve rate is lower than Memoryless because retrieval by symptom similarity sometimes returns irrelevant incidents, misleading the agent.

History-LLM shows another failure mode: active retrieval over unstructured memory can take much longer than no memory. Because one raw history is added after every incident, the search space grows linearly with the stream. As the number of past incidents increases, the agent spends more tokens reading summaries and grepping over potentially relevant trajectories, and more time deciding whether prior incidents apply. Claude Code can spawn nested agents in all configurations, but we observe much more nested-agent use in History-LLM because retrieval itself is delegated to model reasoning. Those nested agents often duplicate relevance checks and Kubernetes probes across similar prior incidents, and the main agent frequently double-checks their findings by reading the flagged trajectories again, incurring high token usage. Trajectory inspection shows an anchoring effect: once an early retrieved history appears relevant, the main agent tends to investigate that history’s hypothesis disproportionately, even when later evidence points elsewhere. It increases context, time, and cost, while also lowering diagnosis and mitigation accuracy.

5.2. Deployment from Source

This experiment tests whether SDO can bring applications from source to deployment, and which design decisions make that process reliable and efficient.

Setup.

For each application in Table 1, we start from a fixed source commit and an empty Kubernetes namespace. Before the experiment, we remove the pre-existing Kubernetes deployment configs and Docker setup in the source repositories to emulate initial deployment of a new application. The agent must infer how to containerize each service, build the images, and connect the services into an end-to-end deployment. We evaluate the performance of the resulting deployment with application-specific load generators against the Kubernetes cluster where the application is deployed.

Metrics.

We report deployment success rate, deployment time, and LLM token use. Deployment time includes authoring service Dockerfiles, building service images, and standing up the services in Kubernetes. We also report false success declarations: cases where the deployer stops and claims success but the external load generator still fails.

Results.

Figure 4 reports the deployment time, iteration count, and token usage of SDO with and without operational memory. Both configurations successfully deploy all 11 applications under an iteration budget of 100. We can see that operational memory reduces deployment time and token use by 47.5%, while reducing iterations by 2.5×\times.

The largest gains are from applications that face complex build and deployment steps, such as train-ticket and socialNetwork. These are applications that use static languages, such as Java and C++, in their microservice implementations, have high service count, and have a complex dependency graph between services. Before the Kubernetes deployment can succeed, the agent must first infer the correct build procedure for each service. Failed builds force it to read compiler or build-system logs, revise Dockerfiles, and retry.

The architecture summary, in particular, preserves the high-level deployment plan across these token-intensive repair loops. Without the summary, agents often spend context rediscovering service roles, build commands, and dependency edges while investigating build errors. These sessions are long enough that the deployer can exhaust the 200k-token context window for Sonnet 4.6, the model used in our evaluation, resulting in compaction and loss of important context. With the summary, SDO records how it expects each service to be built and connected before iterating on low-level failures, so later attempts resume from the deployment structure rather than from raw logs.

Effect of health judge.

We separately ablate the independent health judge. Table 3 reports externally validated deployment success with and without it. An application counts as successful only if the final deployment passes the load generator. Time and token values are means across the 11 deployment applications.

Without the health judge (single-agent), the deployer is too eager to stop: every run eventually declared success, reducing time and token use, yet only four deployments passed external validation. The failed runs were partial deployments. For example, some runs omitted required databases. Some large applications, such as train-ticket, were declared complete before all services were deployed. As the single agent spends more context on build and deployment details, it can lose the high-level health objective and accept local progress as end-to-end success. The independent judge prevents this drift by keeping validation anchored to the user-facing load generator. With the judge, all 11 deployments passed the same external success criterion.

5.3. Memory Transfer

We drill down into how SDO’s memory applies to new incidents in two scenarios. In the overlap case, a new incident repeats a fault SDO has already seen. Does its memory resolve the incident faster and cheaper? In the no-overlap case, a new incident shares nothing with prior memory. Does carrying that memory hurt resolution time, accuracy, or token usage?

Setup.

We divide incidents generated from SREGym’s fault templates into a 50-incident training set and two 30-incident test sets: the overlap set reuses templates from the training set but with different parameter bindings, so each incident repeats a known root cause without being identical, and the no-overlap set shares no templates. We build memory by running SDO on the training set, then freeze it during the test runs so agents cannot modify it, isolating its effect from in-run learning. We compare against Memoryless on both test sets, using the metrics of §5.1.

Results.

On recurring faults, SDO resolves incidents faster and cheaper than Memoryless. In Figure 5(a), SDO’s time-to-resolution and token-usage CDFs lie to the left of Memoryless at every percentile: the median incident resolves in 282 s rather than 584 s and consumes 2.2M rather than 5.4M tokens, resolving 2.1×\times faster and using 2.5×\times fewer tokens. The tail in SDO’s CDFs reflects cases where the agent falls back to open-ended diagnosis and performs similarly to Memoryless; 4 of the 30 incidents fall on this tail.

In contrast, the Memoryless agent spends most time and tokens investigating incidents. Solve rates are similar across Memoryless and SDO agents. A firing detector accelerates resolution but does not guarantee end-to-end success: because each incident composes multiple faults, both Memoryless and SDO agents sometimes diagnose and mitigate only a subset of an incident’s faults, leaving incidents not fully resolved even when a detector surfaced a relevant playbook.

On faults with no overlap to prior memory, SDO maintains accuracy and time-to-resolution similar to those of the Memoryless agents (Figure 5(b)). In 9 of 30 novel incidents, detectors surface playbooks. However, because incidents in this set share no root cause with the training set, every surfaced playbook is a false positive. The agent inspects and discards the false positives without being misled. Accuracy and resolution time are similar to Memoryless (Table 4), so a spurious playbook adds some inspection but does not yield a wrong diagnosis or a slower fix. Because we freeze memory in the test set, SDO agents cannot prune mis-firing detectors as they would in live operation (§5.1).

SDO sees a modest token overhead compared to Memoryless: a 17.7% increase at the median. However, this did not translate to increased time-to-resolution. First, an SDO agent dismissing a suggested diagnosis is not fully wasted work: the agent still learned information about the cluster that is useful for subsequent diagnostic steps within the same incident. Second, we find that the SDO agent writes more analysis scripts than the Memoryless one—in 83% of incidents versus 53% for the Memoryless agent. Scripts can reduce execution time. Rather than issue one command per tool call and wait for its response, the agent batches the requisite commands into a single script and retrieves only the output it needs. Two factors contribute to SDO agents’ propensity to write scripts: (1) SDO agents contain instructions on writing scripts as part of their memory instructions; (2) they see example scripts from the playbooks in frozen operational memory.

5.4. Retrieval Accuracy and Cost

We investigate whether detectors retrieve the right playbooks. Unlike §5.1 and §5.3, which measure end-to-end outcomes, this experiment isolates retrieval: all configurations retrieve from the same playbook corpus learned by SDO, so any difference in accuracy reflects the mechanism rather than the stored memory.

Setup.

We reuse the frozen memory and the overlap and no-overlap test sets of §5.3. On the overlap set, a relevant playbook exists in the corpus, so we report precision and recall over pooled matching decisions. Since an incident can match several playbooks, we pool the true positives, false positives, and false negatives across all incidents. We then compute a single precision and recall from the aggregate counts. On the no-overlap set, no playbook matches the incident, so we report the false-positive rate: the fraction of incidents for which a mechanism surfaces any playbook.

Holding the playbooks fixed, we compare three retrieval mechanisms. Playbook-Embed and Playbook-LLM apply the retrieval mechanisms of History-Embed and History-LLM (§5.1) to SDO’s playbooks instead of raw incident histories, and Detectors uses the agent-authored detector code SDO stores alongside the playbooks. Because the benchmark defines which faults each incident contains, we label the playbooks relevant to each incident as ground truth, then run each mechanism on the retrieval step alone and score what it surfaces against these labels. We score a single retrieval at incident onset; a live end-to-end run instead retrieves repeatedly as the agent tests hypotheses, and SDO’s subsequent retrievals take an LLM-based slow path equivalent to Playbook-LLM.

Results.

Table 5 reports the accuracy and cost of the three mechanisms. Detectors retrieve about as accurately as Playbook-LLM and dominate Playbook-Embed on every metric, while incurring no LLM cost at retrieval time. Embedding is the worst of both worlds: it pays LLM tokens yet retrieves least accurately. Relative to Playbook-LLM, detectors give up some precision in exchange for roughly 45×\times less time and no tokens. Precision is modest in absolute terms across all mechanisms because an incident can match several playbooks and, more importantly, the same symptom often maps to many candidate playbooks with distinct root causes. Retrieval cannot separate these candidates on symptoms alone; discriminating among them is the diagnostic work SDO leaves to the responder, which inspects the live cluster and rejects the playbooks that do not apply (§5.3).

The mechanisms differ in how they find relevant playbooks, which drives both accuracy and cost gaps. Playbook-Embed relies on text similarity, but incidents describe concrete symptoms while playbooks are written generically, so the two share little text and it misses most relevant playbooks. It nonetheless uses LLM tokens: the agent must still explore the cluster to form a query, which costs both time and tokens. Playbook-LLM is more accurate because the agent performs retrieval itself, inspecting live cluster state and correlating it with playbook content by in-context reasoning rather than text overlap. This achieves better accuracy than Detectors at the expense of retrieval time and token cost. Detectors instead encode that correlation in advance: a prior agent writes detector code alongside the playbook, offloading the reasoning into a deterministic predicate over cluster state that hands the next agent a relevant playbook and a starting point to investigate from. Because the predicate runs without an LLM, retrieval costs no tokens; SDO runs each detector twice to exclude transient failures, adding only a 10 s delay across two detector runs.

On the no-overlap set, where no playbook is relevant, embedding surfaces playbooks on every incident because it always returns its top five by similarity, without reasoning about whether they apply. Playbook-LLM avoids spurious retrieval best, followed by detectors, which lack the LLM reasoning to rule out playbooks with similar symptoms and so report a higher false positive rate. §5.3 shows that the SDO agent dismisses these irrelevant playbooks effectively.

6. Related Work

LLM agents for system operations.

A growing line of work applies LLM-based agents to system tasks. Stratus (Chen et al., 2026) diagnoses faults on microservice deployments, with a focus on operational safety; RCACopilot (Chen et al., 2024) predicts a root-cause category for an alert; and FLASH (Zhang et al., 2024) follows human-authored troubleshooting guides to diagnose recurring incidents. Benchmarks such as AIOpsLab (Chen et al., 2025) and ITBench (Jha et al., 2025) evaluate such agents on already-deployed, faulted clusters. Evolutionary systems such as AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025), ADRS (Cheng et al., 2025), and Glia (Hamadanian et al., 2025) instead optimize components by iterating over a population of candidate solutions. These systems either keep state within a single session or consume human-authored knowledge, and the evolutionary ones retain a population but discard negative lessons. SDO instead persists each session as memory that is auditable, directly invocable as agent-authored scripts, and retrieved by checking live cluster state rather than by symptom similarity, so it stays aligned with a continuously changing deployment.

Self-improving LLM agents.

A separate line of work uses environment feedback to improve agents over time. Voyager (Wang et al., 2023) grows an executable skill library; Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) reflects verbally across repeated attempts at the same task; ExpeL (Zhao et al., 2024) and Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al., 2024) distill cross-task lessons as natural-language text; and RLAIF and related techniques fine-tune the model on outcome-derived preferences. Recursive self-improvement systems go further, rewriting their own code or policy to become more capable agents in general: STOP (Zelikman et al., 2023), Gödel Agent (Yin et al., 2024), and the Darwin Gödel Machine (Zhang et al., 2025) edit their own implementation, in the lineage of Schmidhuber’s Gödel machine (Schmidhuber, 2007). SDO accumulates executable artifacts like Voyager rather than the text lessons of Reflexion, ExpeL, and AWM, but its self-definition is deliberately bounded: it holds the model and a fixed detector API constant and revises only a deployment’s operational memory, so unlike the self-rewriting systems every change stays auditable and reversible. Unlike all of this work, SDO operates in production and treats the running cluster as its supervisory signal.

Memory and long context for LLMs.

General-purpose memory systems (Packer et al., 2023) and retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020) externalize knowledge into searchable stores, but optimize for dialogue and question-answering, where the units of memory are short facts retrieved by embedding similarity; serving-layer caches reuse past responses the same way to cut cost (Yu et al., 2025). SDO’s knowledge base differs structurally: a per-application world model grounds every session, and entries are parameterized causal chains with executable scripts, read on demand by a single role, rather than text documents. The parameterized form keeps literal entity names out of the diagnostic context, which is what makes SDO robust to deployment drift where generic RAG over post-mortems is not. Larger context windows do not subsume this: loading raw history into every session is costly, dilutes attention, and still lacks the parameterization needed to survive drift.

Runbooks and incident management.

SDO’s playbooks build on practitioner-authored runbooks and standard operating procedures (Beyer et al., 2016; Beyer et al., 2018), but are authored and refined by the agent itself, parameterized over the deployment’s entities, and coupled with executable scripts. Prior systems recommend an existing human-authored guide for an incident (Jiang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024); SDO instead authors the guidance, while remaining able to import human runbooks as seed material.

7. Conclusion

SDO shows that autonomous operators can improve with experience by turning incident resolutions into operational memory. Across 11 microservice applications, compared to a memoryless agent, SDO achieves the highest end-to-end incident solve rate, reduces application deployment time and token use by up to 47.5%, and resolves recurring faults up to 2.1×\times faster, while using 2.5×\times fewer tokens. These results suggest that the right memory for SRE agents is not raw incident history, but operating procedure: detectors that retrieve applicable knowledge, playbooks that encode reusable repairs, and architecture summaries that keep both grounded in the evolving application.
